catalog_citation: Mortensen, David. 2003. Comparative Tangkhul. Unpublished qualifying paper, University of California, Berkeley, dated 17 December 2003, 73 pp. (the Internet Archive copy ofhttp://www.davidmortensen.org/papers/comparative_tangkhul.pdf,snapshot 20250127).
catalog_locator: sec. 3 'Prefixes' p.11 (numbered list, item 1) and sec. 3.1 'Prefixes and Stress' pp.11-12; examples sec. 3.2 'Prefixes and Tone' p.12 (= printed pages 11-12).
catalog_quote: 1. They do not bear stress, unlike root syllables. ... 3.1 Prefixes and Stress. In Tangkhul languages, stress is always predictable. Only roots bear stress, and prefixes never bear stress. The preferred stress pattern, for a word (and foot), is iambic or anapestic. That is to say, a stem usually consists of a stressed (heavy syllable) root and one or two unstressed (light syllable) prefixes. Suffixes that are not a stem in their own right are not stressed, but these often form part of the same stressed syllable as the root. The unstressed nature of these prefixes is probably the source of their relatively predictable vocalism. In almost all cases, the vowel in a prefix is either a mid-central vowel [@], or a high vowel [i ~ 1]. ... The mid vowel could probably be treated as an allophone of /5/ that occurs in unstressed syllables, but it has been symbolized as @ here in order to facilitate the easy identification of unstressed prefixal syllables. 3.2 Prefixes and Tone. The unstressed prefixes are very short and cannot bear the full range of tonal contrasts observed in the stressed root syllables. [examples, Standard Tangkhul column: 'far' k`@.tà, 'alive' kh`@.rìN, 'warm' kh`@.lùm, 'hear' kh`@.N`@.nà, 'cough' kh`@.N`@.khá, 'lick' kh`@.m`@.lek; periods mark the prefix/root division, so the stressed root is the final syllable] [text-layer note: '@' = schwa, '5' = the stressed root allophone (IPA turned a), 'N' = eng, '1' = barred i; tones are marked, stress is not]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: tang1336 is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title (Blondel & Miller 2000, LSF nursery rhymes) is a Glottolog keyword artefact ('rhymes'), about French Sign Language, irrelevant, priority none. Beyond the item list, five first-hand Tangkhul phonologies held by the project were read (Arokianathan 1987 grammar pp.4,147; CIIL 'Tangkhul-Naga Grammar: A Study of Word Formation' e-book, mislabelled Arokianathan1987 in the sibling folder; Devi 2011 ch.II; Khuraijam 2014 ch.2; plus Gopal 2017, Matisoff 1972, Mortensen & Miller 2013, LSI 1903, the 1995 dictionary): all describe a tone language and none states a word-stress rule; Arokianathan 1987 mentions 'the stress pattern' only as a word-boundary cue. The StressTyp2 'initial stress' source, Arokianathan 1980 Tangkhul Naga Phonetic Reader, was located on Bharatavani (CIIL) but is account-gated ('Login to Read'); not on archive.org; priority high for acquisition. Haobam 2018 (Somdal phonology, Shodhganga 359825) folder exists but is empty, medium priority. Crossref title search found no Tangkhul stress/prosody titles.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only claim of a stress position is the database template: primary stress on the first syllable of every word, no secondary stress. No first-hand description states this. Every first-hand description opened (Arokianathan 1987; Victor 1997; Leisan 2016 Hunphun; Khuraijam 2014 Hundung; Devi 2011 Shangshak; Haobam 2018 Somdal; Meitei 2025 Sikibung/Kasom; Arokianathan & Sharma 1995) treats Tangkhul as a tone language (two or three lexical tones) and lists tone (plus length, nasality or juncture) as the only suprasegmentals; Arokianathan 1987 p.147 alone mentions 'the stress pattern' as a cue to word boundaries without saying where it falls.
new_statements.secondary_stress: StressTyp2 pattern 99: none (ambiguous between 'none reported' and 'verifiably none'). No primary source discusses it.
new_statements.domain_note: Database claim is word-level ('words of all sizes'); no passage, page or example in the dump. The StressTyp2 lect is labelled 'Naga' (iso NULL) and Gordon 2002 files it under 'Creole'; the identity as Tangkhul rests only on the cited source title (Arokianathan 1980 Tangkhul Naga Phonetic Reader). The first-hand tone statements are for citation-form words in the Ukhrul/Hunphun standard (Leisan 2016; Arokianathan 1987) and village lects (Hundung, Shangshak, Somdal, Sikibung, T.M. Kasom).
new_statements.identity_note: Sources cover several Tangkhul village lects: Ukhrul/Hunphun standard (Arokianathan 1987; Victor 1997; Leisan 2016; Gopal 2017; Bhat 1969; Pettigrew 1918), Hundung (Khuraijam 2014), Shangshak (Devi 2011), Somdal (Haobam 2018), Sikibung and T.M. Kasom (Meitei 2025; Kasom may belong to Southern Tangkhul khan1277). The StressTyp2 datum is filed as 'Naga' (language 241, iso NULL) and Gordon 2002 lists it under 'Creole'; it is keyed to tang1336 only through its cited source title (Arokianathan 1980 Tangkhul Naga Phonetic Reader). Glottolog's tang1336 bibliography also carries several computationally mis-assigned 'rhymes' items (Amdo Tibetan, hip-hop, LSF nursery rhymes) that are irrelevant.

new_statements.reading: The fullest first-hand description of Tangkhul by the author of the 1980 Phonetic Reader that StressTyp2 cites for 'initial stress' treats Tangkhul as a three-tone language and gives no word-stress rule at all; 'the stress pattern' appears once, as a cue for word delimitation, with no placement stated. Every other first-hand Tangkhul phonology read in this search of works with stress in the title (CIIL 'Study of Word Formation' e-book; Devi 2011 Shangshak; Khuraijam 2014 Hundung) likewise lists tone (with length/nasality) as the only suprasegmentals and is silent on stress. No primary source read supports a fixed: initial syllable word-stress claim for Tangkhul; the one text that could (Arokianathan 1980 Phonetic Reader) is login-gated on Bharatavani.

tone_statements.quote: Tone is phonemic in Lunghar variety. Lunghar is a tonal language with 4 contrastive lexical tones; two level tones (low and mid) and two contour tones (rising and falling). Using the Chao tone number system (Chao, 1930), the Falling Tone is realised at a pitch level of [55]/[44] to [11]; the rising tone is realised from [11] to [33]; the mid tone has its focus at [33]; and the low tone is realised at [11]/[22]. … The four lexical tonemes are not restricted to specific syllable types, nor to initial consonant types or to specific word classes.
tone_statements.locator: p. 85, sec. 5 Tone / 5.1 Toneme + Table 10 'Contrastive tonemes' (also sec. 4 pp. 83-84 obligatory tone in the syllable; sec. 6.3 pp. 87-88 F0 Table 13; sec. 7 p. 88; note 4 p. 89 TBU)
tone_statements.summary: Lunghar (village variety of Tangkhul): four contrastive tones, level low and mid plus falling and rising, on every syllable; F0 measured; the author says Standard Tangkhul has no falling tone.

tone_statements.quote: SKT and TMKT varieties are the two varieties of Tangkhul which is a tone language. In Tangkhul, meaning of a word can be changed with relative pitch. Based on the fieldwork conducted by researcher, it is confirmed that both the language varieties have three contrastive level tones i.e. rising, falling and mid tones. According to S. Arokianathan (1987), standard Tangkhul variety has three contrastive tones i.e. level or mid, rising and falling tones. Hyman (2014) also mentioned that Tangkhul has three contrastive tones. SKT and TMKT also have three level ways of tonal contrasts in isolation; a) Rising Tone (MH) b) Mid Tone (M), and c) Falling Tone (HL). [...] Tone bearing unit (TBU) of SKT and TMKT is the rhyme of a syllable.

tone_statements.quote: An example of type A is Tangkhul Naga [Tibeto-Burman; NE India], which has no tonal morphology or tonal alternations; the three contrastive tones /H/, /M/ and /L/ on lexical morphemes which just stay on their own syllables and do not interact: páay ‘defecate’, pā ay ‘be cheap, able’, pàay ‘jump’. This non-interaction is largely attributable to the fact that toneless grammatical morphemes intervene between the lexical roots whose tones thus rarely meet when words are concatenated. This includes a certain number of toneless lexicalized prefixes, as seen on the following nouns and verbs [personal notes]:
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones H, M, L, contrastive on lexical root syllables only; prefixes and grammatical morphemes toneless; no grammatical tone, no sandhi or tone rules.

tone_statements.citation: Matisoff, James A. 1972. Tangkhul Naga and comparative Tibeto-Burman. Tonan Ajia Kenkyu (東南アジア研究 / Southeast Asian Studies, Kyoto) 10(2): 271-283.
tone_statements.quote: There are three tones, high-falling /’/, low-falling /*/, and an unmarked tone, presumably mid. ... In any event, it is obvious that tone does not play as vital a role in distinguishing TN utterances (or Kukish utterances in general) as it does in such phonologically degenerate branches of Tibeto-Burman as Lolo-Burmese. In spite of clear contrasts (e.g. athay-rm ‘fruit juice’ vs. athay-ri ‘fruit pip’), there is much tonal variation among different occurrences of the same morpheme according to the particular compounds in which it appears.
tone_statements.locator: p.272 (end of sec. (a) on Bhat's Introduction) and p.273 first paragraph
tone_statements.summary: 3 lexical tones on the (root) syllable per Bhat 1969: high-falling, low-falling, unmarked mid; low functional load; tone of a morpheme varies across compounds; no proto-tones reconstructed.

This non-interaction is largely attributable to the fact that toneless grammatical morphemes intervene between the lexical roots whose tones thus rarely meet when words are concatenated. sources.note: Classifies Tangkhul Naga as a type A ('lethargic') tone system: three contrastive tones /H/, /M/, /L/ on lexical morphemes, no tonal morphology and no tonal alternations; tones stay on their own syllables and do not interact, which Hyman attributes to toneless grammatical morphemes (and toneless lexicalized prefixes aa-, ma-, ka-, nga-) intervening between lexical roots; illustrated with páay 'defecate' / pāay 'be cheap, able' / pàay 'jump' and twelve prefixed nouns/verbs sorted by root tone (aa-kúy 'head', aa-kōr 'cover', aa-khòŋ 'neck', etc.).

sources.citation: Matisoff, James A. 1972. Tangkhul Naga and comparative Tibeto-Burman. Tonan Ajia Kenkyu (東南アジア研究 / Southeast Asian Studies, Kyoto) 10(2): 271-283.
sources.quote: There are three tones, high-falling /’/, low-falling /*/, and an unmarked tone, presumably mid. ... In any event, it is obvious that tone does not play as vital a role in distinguishing TN utterances (or Kukish utterances in general) as it does in such phonologically degenerate branches of Tibeto-Burman as Lolo-Burmese. In spite of clear contrasts (e.g. athay-rm ‘fruit juice’ vs. athay-ri ‘fruit pip’), there is much tonal variation among different occurrences of the same morpheme according to the particular compounds in which it appears.
